title: vSV-ViT: Variable-size SuperVertex Vision Transformer for Cortical Surface Learning in Alzheimer's Disease
abstract: arXiv:2605.26514v3 Announce Type: replace-cross  Abstract: Learning from 3D meshes is challenging because the data reside on non-Euclidean surfaces embedded in 3D space. This is particularly evident in domains such as brain cortical surface analysis, where existing models typically rely on ROI-agnostic, face-based, or fixed-size patches. Such patches can duplicate boundary vertices, conflate anatomically distinct regions, or incorporate non-cortical vertices such as those of the medial wall. We develop variable-size supervertex (vSV) partitioning, which groups cortical surface vertices into vSV patches similar to superpixels in images. Building on these vSVs, we design Variable-size SuperVertex Vision Transformer (vSV-ViT), a Vision Transformer that processes vSVs through padding, mask-aware patch embedding, and vertex position embedding. We demonstrate the benefits of the proposed framework through a quantitative analysis of vertex assignment in surface partitioning and downstream tas

translated_title: vSV-ViT：用于阿尔茨海默病皮层表面学习的可变尺寸超顶点视觉Transformer
translated_abstract: 从3D网格中学习具有挑战性，因为数据位于嵌入3D空间的非欧几里得曲面上。这在诸如大脑皮层表面分析等领域尤为明显，现有模型通常依赖于与感兴趣区域无关的、基于面片的或固定大小的补丁。此类补丁可能复制边界顶点、混淆解剖学上不同的区域，或包含非皮层顶点（如内侧壁的顶点）。我们开发了可变尺寸超顶点（vSV）分区方法，将皮层表面顶点分组为类似于图像中超像素的vSV补丁。基于这些vSV，我们设计了可变尺寸超顶点视觉Transformer（vSV-ViT），这是一种通过填充、掩码感知补丁嵌入和顶点位置嵌入来处理vSV的视觉Transformer。我们通过对表面分区中顶点分配的定量分析和下游任务展示了所提出框架的优势。
tldr: 本文提出可变尺寸超顶点（vSV）分区方法和vSV-ViT视觉Transformer，通过将皮层表面顶点分组为可变大小的补丁，并采用填充、掩码感知补丁嵌入和顶点位置嵌入进行处理，解决了传统固定大小补丁方法在阿尔茨海默病皮层表面分析中复制边界顶点、混淆解剖区域和包含非皮层顶点的问题。
en_tdlr: This paper proposes variable-size supervertex (vSV) partitioning and vSV-ViT, a Vision Transformer that groups cortical surface vertices into variable-size patches and processes them through padding, mask-aware patch embedding, and vertex position embedding, addressing the limitations of traditional ROI-agnostic, face-based, or fixed-size patch methods in cortical surface analysis for Alzheimer's disease.
